Fresh Hand-Churned Imbolc Butter

Served at: Imbolc Eve (La Fheile Bride)

Approximately 1/2 pound (225g)Prep 20 min

Imbolc, or La Fheile Bride, marks the halfway point between the winter solstice and the spring equinox, celebrating the first stirrings of spring and the return of light. Traditionally, this is a time when ewes begin to lactate, making fresh dairy products like butter a symbolic and nourishing offering to Brigid, the Celtic goddess of hearth, home, and fertility. Making your own butter is a simple, satisfying way to connect with this ancient tradition and welcome the season's renewal.

Ingredients

  • 1 pint (470ml) heavy cream (at least 36% milkfat), very cold
  • 1/4 teaspoon fine sea salt, or to taste (optional)
  • 1 cup (240ml) ice water, for washing

Method

  1. Ensure your cream, mixing bowl (if using a stand mixer), and whisk attachment or jar are very cold. You can chill them in the refrigerator for at least 30 minutes prior.
  2. Pour the very cold heavy cream into a clean, chilled quart-sized (1-liter) jar with a tight-fitting lid, or into the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment.
  3. If using a jar, shake vigorously. If using a stand mixer, beat on medium-high speed. The cream will first thicken into whipped cream, then become grainy.
  4. Continue shaking or beating. Eventually, the milk solids (butter) will separate from the liquid (buttermilk). This can take anywhere from 5 to 15 minutes of active shaking or mixing. You will hear a sloshing sound as the butter forms a solid mass.
  5. Once the butter has clearly separated, pour the contents through a fine-mesh sieve or colander lined with cheesecloth into a bowl to collect the buttermilk. Reserve the buttermilk for baking or drinking.
  6. Transfer the butter solids to a clean, chilled bowl. Pour about 1/2 cup (120ml) of ice water over the butter. Using a spatula or your clean hands, gently press and fold the butter, squeezing out any remaining buttermilk. The water will become cloudy.
  7. Drain the cloudy water and repeat the washing process with fresh ice water, pressing and folding, until the water runs clear. This step is crucial for removing all buttermilk, which can cause the butter to spoil quickly.
  8. Once the water runs clear, drain thoroughly. If using, sprinkle the salt over the butter and knead it in until evenly distributed.
  9. Shape the butter into a log or block using your spatula or hands. Wrap tightly in parchment paper or plastic wrap and refrigerate.

Tips

  • For faster churning, ensure your cream is as cold as possible, ideally straight from the back of the refrigerator.
  • The reserved buttermilk is excellent for pancakes, biscuits, or drinking. Store it in the refrigerator for up to a week.
  • Experiment with flavorings by kneading in fresh herbs like chives or dill, or a pinch of garlic powder after salting.
